table.header: Abstract

table.text: This demonstrates that participants were sensitive to social affordances, specifically opponents' interception potential, shaped by postural information through facing direction when judging the minimum gap width they could successfully kick through.
table.header: Introduction

table.text: Participants were recruited through university football clubs, social media and posters.
table.header: Participants

table.text: All participants were male Tier 2 athletes (Mckay et al., 2021) training at least three times per week to compete locally, with no history of motor, learning-related or neurological conditions, and no moderate to severe injury in the last three months, ensuring a coherent sample of comparable ability.

table.text: Prior to testing, participants were given 10 minutes to conduct a self-led dynamic warm up, reducing the risk of muscular injury (Perez-Gomez, 2020).
table.header: Procedure

table.text: Prior to the first trial, participants were verbally instructed by the experimenter to only attempt an interception if they believed they would get to the ball ahead of their opponent, and informed that movements of more than two steps towards the ball would be recorded as an interception attempt.
table.header: Procedure

table.text: In study 1, participants completed 3 trials against their opponent at each target marker, with the order counterbalanced for each participant using a Latin Square and a Mirrored Latin Square, accounting for order effects.

table.header: Participants consistently made proactive interceptive decisions.

table.text: As shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2d, participants were more likely to attempt interceptive action, and succeed, when the oncoming ball was closer to them than their opponent, (i.e., when the distance ratio decreased).

table.text: As shown in Figure 3e and Figure 3f, participants were more likely to attempt interceptive action and succeed when they had a distance advantage over their opponent at each ball speed.

table.header: Ball speed amplifies the spatial constraints on interceptive success.

table.text: As ball speed increased, participants were less likely to attempt an interception, highlighting that they were sensitive to the reduced time available when making interceptive decisions at higher ball speeds.
table.header: Ball speed amplifies the spatial constraints on interceptive success.

table.header: Proactive interceptive behaviour persists, while additional load produces asymmetric effects

table.text: This highlights that participants were sensitive to the changes in their own and their opponents movement capabilities, when making interceptive decisions.
table.header: Load independently influences interceptive decisions and outcomes alongside spatial constraints.

table.text: However, as participants had no explicit awareness of the specific load condition on each trial, and no opportunity to explore their action capabilities before or between trials, any influence of visual and proprioceptive cues was likely minimal and non-specific.
table.header: General Discussion

table.text: Exploratory evidence suggests that participants are sensitive to increases in target distance and additional load, even on a trial-by-trial basis, but less sensitive to changes in target speed.

> As ball speed increased, participants were less likely to attempt an interception, highlighting that they were sensitive to the reduced time available when making interceptive decisions at higher ball speeds.

> If participants are sensitive to the changes in their own, and their opponents, movement velocity brought on by additional load (Macadam et al., 2019), then they should attempt less interceptions when the load reduces their ability to reach the ball and attempt more when the load impacts their opponents' abilities.

> Accordingly, we hypothesised that mean PSE would be significantly different at each additional load condition, with higher PSEs when opponents are under load and lower PSEs when participants are under load.

> As shown in Figure 4b, outcome-based PSEs were significantly greater than 1.0 across conditions (V = 2227, p = .028, r = 0.24), and when opponents were under load (-5kg: V = 120, p = .042, r = 0.50; -10kg: V = 114, p = .002, r = 0.79) indicating that participants were more successful when opponents were under load.

> This highlights that participants were sensitive to the changes in their own and their opponents movement capabilities, when making interceptive decisions.

> However, as participants had no explicit awareness of the specific load condition on each trial, and no opportunity to explore their action capabilities before or between trials, any influence of visual and proprioceptive cues was likely minimal and non-specific.

> Exploratory evidence suggests that participants are sensitive to increases in target distance and additional load, even on a trial-by-trial basis, but less sensitive to changes in target speed.

For studies 2 and 3, a moderate to large effect size of target speed, and additional load was used (Cohen's D = 0.65) to be conservative while reflecting previous research finding strong effects of target speed on interceptive affordances (Barte et al., 2018), and additional load on affordances for the self and others (Walter et al., 2019). report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .156", "p ≥.489", "p ≥.601", "p =.052"), Sentence = c("Outcome-based PSEs (i.e successful interceptions) were not significantly different from 1.0, t(15) = -1.49, p = .156, d = -0.37, BF = 0.65 ± 0.02%., and decision-based PSEs were significantly greater than outcomebased PSEs, t(15) = 7.17, p <.001, d = 1.79, BF = 6141.34 ± 0%.", "Outcome-based PSEs did not significantly differ from 1.0 across or within ball speed conditions (p ≥.489) suggesting that interception outcomes may have been primarily constrained by relative target distance, rather than ball speed.", "Conversely, outcome-based PSEs did not differ between ball speed conditions as revealed by Holm-corrected pairwise comparisons (p ≥.601).", "Ball speed approached significance for trial outcomes (β = -0.15, p =.052), but did not significantly predict action decisions, nor was there a significant interaction between distance ratio and ball speed predicting action decisions." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. This demonstrates that participants were sensitive to social affordances, specifically opponents' interception potential, shaped by postural information through facing direction when judging the minimum gap width they could successfully kick through.
Participants were recruited through university football clubs, social media and posters.

All participants were male Tier 2 athletes (Mckay et al., 2021) training at least three times per week to compete locally, with no history of motor, learning-related or neurological conditions, and no moderate to severe injury in the last three months, ensuring a coherent sample of comparable ability.
Participants were given an inconvenience allowance for their time.
For each testing session, participants were paired with another individual from the participant pool who acted as the opponent during the session.
Prior to testing, participants were given 10 minutes to conduct a self-led dynamic warm up, reducing the risk of muscular injury (Perez-Gomez, 2020).

Prior to the first trial, participants were verbally instructed by the experimenter to only attempt an interception if they believed they would get to the ball ahead of their opponent, and informed that movements of more than two steps towards the ball would be recorded as an interception attempt.

In study 1, participants completed 3 trials against their opponent at each target marker, with the order counterbalanced for each participant using a Latin Square and a Mirrored Latin Square, accounting for order effects.
In study 2, participants completed 6 trials per position.
In study 3 participants completed 10 trials per position.
Participants completed each study during separate testing sessions.

The order in which participants completed each study was counterbalanced by repeating the six possible study orders in a fixed sequence across participants, then alternating study orders across participants only completing studies 2 and 3. (a) Depiction of the experimental set up detailing the positions of participant and opponent starting points, target markers, and the Football Delivery Machine, as well as the distances between them. (b) Calculation of the distance to the target marker for the participant (purple) and the opponent (orange) with Pythagorean theorem using position 1 as an example.

Nevertheless, this pattern suggests that participants were successful only up to the point that neither player held a spatial advantage, indicating that the proactive action strategy adopted by participants did not correspond with their interceptive success.

As shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2d, participants were more likely to attempt interceptive action, and succeed, when the oncoming ball was closer to them than their opponent, (i.e., when the distance ratio decreased).
This indicates that participants were sensitive to the spatial constraints of their environment when making interceptive decisions.
However, study 1 does not examine whether participants are sensitive to the temporal constraints of their environment.

If participants are sensitive to the temporal constraints of the environment, then they should perceive that they have less time to execute a successful interceptive action when the ball is moving more quickly and therefore be less likely to attempt interceptive action.
As shown in Figure 3e and Figure 3f, participants were more likely to attempt interceptive action and succeed when they had a distance advantage over their opponent at each ball speed.

As ball speed increased, participants were less likely to attempt an interception, highlighting that they were sensitive to the reduced time available when making interceptive decisions at higher ball speeds.

If participants are sensitive to the changes in their own, and their opponents, movement velocity brought on by additional load (Macadam et al., 2019), then they should attempt less interceptions when the load reduces their ability to reach the ball and attempt more when the load impacts their opponents' abilities.

Accordingly, we hypothesised that mean PSE would be significantly different at each additional load condition, with higher PSEs when opponents are under load and lower PSEs when participants are under load.

As shown in Figure 4b, outcome-based PSEs were significantly greater than 1.0 across conditions (V = 2227, p = .028, r = 0.24), and when opponents were under load (-5kg: V = 120, p = .042, r = 0.50; -10kg: V = 114, p = .002, r = 0.79) indicating that participants were more successful when opponents were under load.
This highlights that participants were sensitive to the changes in their own and their opponents movement capabilities, when making interceptive decisions.

However, as participants had no explicit awareness of the specific load condition on each trial, and no opportunity to explore their action capabilities before or between trials, any influence of visual and proprioceptive cues was likely minimal and non-specific.
Exploratory evidence suggests that participants are sensitive to increases in target distance and additional load, even on a trial-by-trial basis, but less sensitive to changes in target speed.

text.text: To perform well, athletes must perceive both individual and social affordances within sporting environments.
Interceptive action is often crucial to sporting success, yet research investigating interceptive affordance perception in open-play competitive sporting environments is extremely limited.
This novel research investigates how factors such as target distance, target speed, and additional load jointly influence affordance perception for interceptive actions against opponents.

Across three pre-registered studies, university level footballers (n = 26) made action-based judgments on whether they could successfully intercept a target moving perpendicularly towards the space between themselves and an opponent.
The position of the target systematically varied in its proximity to the participant versus the opponent.
Participants consistently displayed proactive interceptive behaviour, persisting with manipulations to target speed, and additional load applied to players and opponents.
However, exploratory mixed-effects modelling revealed that participants were sensitive to increases in relative target distance, and additional load, but less sensitive to increases in target speed.

These findings have wide ranging implications across many sporting and non-sporting contexts, providing new insights to understanding affordance perception in competitive sporting situations and other fast-paced environments.
Additionally, this work has practical applications, highlighting opportunities to explore coaching interventions to enhance interceptive decision-making during matches.

Interceptive actions have been widely investigated in many everyday domains from collision avoidance in traffic situations (Chihak et al., 2014; Louveton et al., 2012), or navigating busy crowds (Taylor & Cinelli, 2021; Meerhoff et al., 2018), to catching, striking, tackling and blocking in sports such as baseball (Gray et al., 2025, Ranganathan and Carlton, 2007), cricket (Mann et al., 2010 , Runswick et al., 2018), tennis (Rosker & Majcen Rosker, 2021; Sáenz-Moncaleano et al., 2018), football (Travassos et al., 2012 , Zheng et al., 2021), and rugby (Brault et al., 2012; Passos et al., 2008).

text.text: For any perceptual-motor control process to perform efficiently, the perceiver must have access to information that informs: 1) when they should attempt to perform an action, and arguably more importantly, 2) when they should not.

Visual information processing such as object processing and spatial processing provides perceivers with cues about the properties of their environment and the objects within it (Adaval et al., 2018), informing the actions that the perceiver could potentially undertake (Cisek, 2007; Tucker & Ellis, 1998).

text.text: For example, In the case of football interception players perceive information within the environment-such as ball speed, trajectory and distance-and use that information to guide action.
Here the key question is not simply "How fast is the ball?"
but "Can I successfully act on this ball?".
As informational variables in the environment change during ball flight, players must prospectively adjust their movements to ensure the interception remains possible-"Can I still act on this ball?".
According to affordance theory, the ball presents an affordance for interception if the player perceives that it is possible to reach it.

The interception affordance continues to exist up until the point that the ball is no longer possible to reach, at which point the player should pursue a different course of action, an example of affordance-based control (Fajen, 2005).

In a second study, Peker et al. (2023) found a three-way interaction when additionally manipulating facing direction (whether players were facing inward towards the gap or outwards away from the gap).

This demonstrates that participants were sensitive to social affordances, specifically opponents' interception potential, shaped by postural information through facing direction when judging the minimum gap width they could successfully kick through.

Sporting environments are highly dynamic and unpredictable, requiring athletes to perform highly technical and complex actions, adhering to sport specific rules, while their personal and social affordances are constantly changing (Fajen et al., 2008).

text.text: A ubiquitous, yet vital action in many sports is interception: the act of preventing an object from continuing its trajectory.
A substantial body of research examining the informational basis of interceptive behaviour suggests that interceptive actions are primarily guided by early ball flight information.

Work in tennis (Triolet et al., 2013; Shim et al., 2005), cricket (Runswick et al., 2018), and baseball (Ranganathan & Carlton, 2007) shows that postural cues support the preparation of movement, primarily through stepping patterns, while the initiation and accuracy of interceptive action is based predominantly on early ball flight information.

text.text: Similarly, North et al., (2009) found that footballers anticipate pass outcomes more accurately in the absence of postural cues.

text.text: Although, postural cues become crucial under severe temporal constraints such as penalty kicks (Dicks et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2021).

text.text: Nevertheless, this research underscores the importance of early-ball flight information for interceptive actions in the absence of severe temporal constraints.

Successful interceptive action requires athletes to continuously perceive personal and social affordances, as well as regulate the initiation or withholding of actions based on whether they are afforded to the individual (Marinovic et al., 2009).

text.text: For example, a ball that was perceived as hittable for a baseball player when pitched, may no longer be hittable during flight, depending on the type of pitch used (fastball, curveball, changeup, slider etc).
It is crucial that the baseball player can perceive this changed affordance and suppress their original motor response to prevent a strikeout or a mishit (Gray, 2025).

text.text: In football specifically, interceptive action allows teams to foil opposition attacks, regain possession from the opposing team, and subsequently launch their own attacks to score points.
However, unsuccessful interception attempts leave space for opposing teams to attack and exploit.

Players must perceive informational variables such as ball speed, distance, and trajectory and use that information to guide action. Travassos et al. (2012) conducted time series analyses on intercepted and non-intercepted passes in futsal (five a side indoor football) and found that spatial constraints such as defenders' distances to the ball trajectory determined their interceptive success.

text.text: Although, it remains unclear how target speed impacts interception decisions in the presence of a real opponent, who possesses the real threat of acting on their affordances.

Previous work on interceptive decision-making in football has typically focused on single informational constraints (e.g target speed), and as such has yet to capture how the combined manipulation of multiple informational variables and action capabilities shapes both the perceived and actual boundary at which interception is no longer possible against a live opponent.

The present research aims to address these gaps by using the Point of Subjective Equality (PSE: the point at which performers judge interceptive success and failure as equally likely) (Liuna & Dongjun, 2024) to capture the perceptual boundary at which interception is no longer possible, under manipulations to target distance, target speed, and additional load against a live opponent.

text.text: Greater understanding of how footballers perceive their interceptive affordances could have implications for training and coaching interventions, leading to improved athletic performance (de Pinho et al., 2020).

text.text: Beyond football, the present research addresses a broader psychological question concerning how performers perceive the boundaries for action opportunities, under changing informational constraints and disturbances to action capabilities, providing valuable insights into the processes underlying affordance perception in fast-paced interpersonal environments (Azam et al., 2024).

text.text: This research examines how the combined manipulation of informational variables and individual action capabilities shape the perception of interceptive affordances across three separate studies.
Study 1 isolates the effect of relative target distance on interceptive decision-making when presented with an oncoming ball against an opponent.
Study 2 investigates the joint effects of relative target distance and target speed, while study 3 examines the joint effects of relative target distance and additional load.
Across the three studies, we hypothesised that PSE would reflect the actor with the theoretical interception advantage.
Specifically, in study 1 we hypothesised that the PSE would occur when the participant and their opponent were equidistant from the oncoming ball trajectory.

In study 2 we hypothesised that the PSE would shift closer to the participant at slower ball speeds, and closer to the opponent at higher ball speeds, while we hypothesised in study 3 that the PSE would shift closer to whichever actor (participant or opponent) was wearing additional load.
Together, these studies map how the perceptual boundary for interceptive affordance perception shifts under differing constraints.
Sample size was calculated a-priori using G*Power 3.1.9.7 (Faul et al., 2009).

text.text: For all studies, the required power (1-β) was set at .9 and the significance level (α) set to .05.

For study 1, a large effect size was used while being conservative (Cohen's D = 0.8) based on findings from Travassos et al. (2012) who found a large effect of defender distance to ball trajectory when observing interceptive actions in futsal.

text.text: For studies 2 and 3, a moderate to large effect size of target speed, and additional load was used (Cohen's D = 0.65) to be conservative while reflecting previous research finding strong effects of target speed on interceptive affordances (Barte et al., 2018), and additional load on affordances for the self and others (Walter et al., 2019).

text.text: For the parameters defined, a sample size of n = 15 was required for study 1, and n = 22 for studies 2 and 3.
However, the stopping rule was set at n = 20 for study 1, and n = 26 for studies 2 and 3, to allow for potential outliers, participant drop out and/or experimenter error.
Participants were recruited through university football clubs, social media and posters.

Player vs opponent distance-to-ball ratios were calculated for the five target markers by dividing the distance between the participant and the target marker, by the distance between the opponent and the target marker.

text.text: Therefore, the distance ratio provides a relational measure of the spatial advantages or disadvantages at ball release.

To determine how participants' action decisions were influenced by distance to ball ratio, we calculated the point of subjective equality (PSE) for each participant, representing the distance ratio at which the probability of the participant attempting an interception was 0.5.
Decision-based PSE for each participant was calculated by performing a binomial linear model predicting participants' action decision (intercept vs defend) against distance ratio.
A PSE <1.0 indicated more cautious interceptive behaviour, as the oncoming ball was closer to the participant than the opponent when their probability of attempting an interception was 0.5.

text.text: Likewise, a PSE >1.0 indicated more proactive interceptive behaviour, as the oncoming ball was closer to the opponent when participant probability of interceptive behaviour was at 0.5.

text.text: A PSE of 1.0 indicated that the oncoming ball was equidistant between the participant and the opponent when the probability of participants attempting an interception was at 0.5.

To determine how trial outcomes were influenced by distance ratio, we removed trials in which participants did not attempt an interception and then performed another binomial linear model for each participant predicting participant trial outcomes (successful vs unsuccessful interceptions) against distance ratio.
The distance ratio at which the probability was 0.5 was taken as the outcome-based PSE.

Due to the structural properties of the outcome-based data, specifically the reduced and asymmetrical number of observations per participant leading to instances of non-estimable psychometric functions (PSEs could not be reliably estimated) and unstable model fits, interpretations based on outcome-based PSEs are made cautiously.
All statistical analyses were performed using RStudio (version 4.5.2).
Prior to analysis, outliers were removed using median absolute deviation, which involved removing participants with PSE scores ± 3 absolute deviations from the median.
This approach ensured that the outlier identification process was less influenced by extremely large or non-estimable PSEs (Leys et al., 2013).

text.text: For study 1, a one-sample t-test was conducted to investigate whether PSEs across participants differed significantly from 1.0 (the point at which the oncoming ball is equidistant between the participant and opponent).
For studies 2 and 3, Holm corrected one-sample t-tests were conducted investigating whether PSEs for each condition, and across conditions, differed significantly from 1.0.
To determine whether PSEs varied significantly between conditions, one-way repeated measures ANOVAs were conducted comparing PSEs across conditions.
Holm-Bonferroni corrections were also applied to these analyses to control for multiple comparisons.
The above analyses were conducted for both decision-based and outcome-based PSEs.

text.text: Study 1 demonstrated that participants exhibited proactive interceptive behaviour, while their action decisions were strongly influenced by the distance ratio.
This indicates that participants were sensitive to the spatial constraints of their environment when making interceptive decisions.
However, study 1 does not examine whether participants are sensitive to the temporal constraints of their environment.
To address this, study 2 aimed to investigate the effects of target speed on interceptive decision-making against an opponent.

If participants are sensitive to the temporal constraints of the environment, then they should perceive that they have less time to execute a successful interceptive action when the ball is moving more quickly and therefore be less likely to attempt interceptive action.
Accordingly, we hypothesised that mean PSE would be significantly different at each ball speed, with higher PSEs at lower ball speeds and lower PSEs at higher ball speeds.

text.text: Study 2 replicated the pattern of proactive interceptive behaviour from study 1, yet interceptive action decisions were systematically influenced by the temporal constraints of the environment.

As ball speed increased, participants were less likely to attempt an interception, highlighting that they were sensitive to the reduced time available when making interceptive decisions at higher ball speeds.
However, interception success did not vary between ball speeds suggesting that temporal constraints alone did not affect the outcome of interception decisions.
Instead, both spatial and temporal constraints appear to have interacted to affect interceptive success.
These findings build on study 1, showing that participants jointly use spatial and temporal information to make interception decisions.
Nevertheless, study 2 leaves open the question of how interception decisions are shaped by disturbances to one's action capabilities.
To address this, study 3 aimed to investigate how additional load impacts interceptive decision-making.

If participants are sensitive to the changes in their own, and their opponents, movement velocity brought on by additional load (Macadam et al., 2019), then they should attempt less interceptions when the load reduces their ability to reach the ball and attempt more when the load impacts their opponents' abilities.

Across three separate studies, this research aimed to investigate the effects of target distance, target speed, and additional load on interceptive actions using a novel interceptive decision-making task.

Study 1 explored the hypothesis that participants would be sensitive to the relative advantages/disadvantages arising from differences in target distance and therefore the mean PSE would occur when neither the participant nor the opponent had a distance advantage.

Study 2 explored the hypothesis that participants would be sensitive to the tighter temporal constraints of the environment at higher ball speeds and therefore PSEs would be greater at lower ball speeds than higher ball speeds.

Lastly, in study 3, we explored the hypothesis that participants would be sensitive to the changes in their action capabilities brought on by additional load and therefore PSEs would increase as the additional load shifted from the participants to their opponents.

The findings from all three studies demonstrate that participants consistently used a proactive action strategy, readily initiating interception attempts even when at a distance disadvantage relative to their opponents.
These attempts were often unsuccessful indicating that participants may have been prone to overestimating their interceptive ability.

These findings corroborate research by Quammen et al. (2025) who found initial overestimations in interceptive ability across footballers, which decreased over time during an interceptive decision-making task.

text.text: In the present task, where the opponent is a live actor, error-based feedback is especially important to evaluate not only task constraints, but to evaluate how the opponents' action capabilities relate to their own.

The low-risk nature of the task also provides a conducive environment for the use of error-based feedback, due to the lack of negative consequences for interception errors, allowing participants to fully explore the affordance landscape at no detriment to themselves or any teammates.

text.text: The present work contributes to affordance theory by demonstrating how perceptual boundaries shift under manipulation to specifying informational variables and individual action capabilities during fast-paced interceptive tasks.

Our findings align with research on interceptive actions, as well as broader work demonstrating altered behaviour when informational variables change (Quammen et al., 2025; Travassos et al., 2012; Azam et al., 2024), or with disturbances to individual action capabilities (Barte et al., 2018; Gotardi et al., 2024).

text.text: However, the present work also reveals a more complex relationship, whereby perceptual boundaries emerge from the integration of multiple informational and task constraints, and shift in relation to changes in these constraints.

The findings support ecological accounts of behaviour, supporting the notion that affordances are relational and adaptive, continuously shifting in response to changing actor-environment relations (Stoffregen, 2004).

text.text: From an applied perspective, these findings support the use of constraints-based coaching interventions, highlighting that decision-making within football is heavily influenced by environmental and task constraints.

Further empirical evidence documents the positive effects that constraints-based manipulations have on decision-making behaviour (Corrêa et al., 2012; Davids et al., 2013; Ometto et al., 2018; de Pinho et al., 2020).

text.text: Though, it is important to note limitations of this research.
The use of a forced choice decision-making task (Raab & Johnson, 2004) does not capture the richness of competitive environments with the wide array of actions available to athletes.

text.text: Additionally, the present task does not fully capture the multitude of match contexts in which these interceptive actions may occur.
Future research should investigate how contextual factors, such as game score or time remaining, impact perceptual boundaries in open-play football (Loffing & Cañal-Bruland, 2017).

text.text: In conclusion, this research demonstrates that participants display proactive behaviour during an interceptive decision-making task across varying spatial and temporal constraints and under disturbances to action capabilities.
Exploratory evidence suggests that participants are sensitive to increases in target distance and additional load, even on a trial-by-trial basis, but less sensitive to changes in target speed.

These findings suggest that footballers behave in a way that enables continuous evaluation of their maximal action capabilities, while being highly sensitive to spatial constraints but less sensitive to spatio-temporal constraints.
Together, the studies provide a foundation for understanding how athletes perceive their interceptive affordances in competitive contexts.
Future work should explore the role of kinematic and contextual information on perceptual boundaries and explore coaching interventions to enhance real-time decision-making during matches.

In the present study, the lack of kinematic cues from a live passer may have restricted the temporal information available to participants prior to ball release, disrupting early movement preparation, leading to an overreliance on spatial information to make interception decisions.
Future research should investigate the role of kinematic information from the ball carrier on interception decisions in football (Runswick et al., 2018; Savelsbergh et al., 2002).

However, given the exploratory finding, further research is required to validate the perceptual mismatch and determine whether it reflects an inability to use early temporal information usually conveyed by kinematic cues from a live kicker, late temporal information conveyed by unfolding spatialtemporal relationships, or an interaction between the two.
